"It is not yet possible.
The wood is still green;
if plaster is applied on top of it,
it will surely warp.
If green wood is used to build a house,
it may be good now,
but it will certainly collapse later."
Gāoyáng Yīng 高陽應 said,
"That is not so.
According to your words,
the house will not collapse.
As the wood dries, it becomes stronger;
as the plaster dries, it becomes lighter.
Using greater strength to bear less weight, it will not collapse."
The craftsman had no reply,
Received an order and acted accordingly.
The initial construction of the house was good,
but later it ultimately failed.
Gāoyáng 髙陽 was indeed fond of petty observations,
but did not comprehend great principles.
Jì'ào 驥驁, Lǜ'ěr 綠耳 turned their backs to the sun and galloped westward,
but by evening, the sun was still in front of them.
The eye inherently has things it cannot see,
intelligence inherently has things it does not know,
and calculation inherently has things it cannot reach.
Without knowing the explanation of why it is so,
the sage then followed and established regulations,
not concerning himself with intellectualizing.
25.3 *Yǒu Dù* 《有度》
Three things:
An enlightened ruler listens with measure,
therefore he does not overstep.
To listen with measure,
then he cannot be deceived,
cannot be alarmed,
cannot be frightened,
cannot be delighted.
With the knowledge of ordinary people,
they are not confused by what they already know,
but are confused by what they do not know,
Zé rén zhī yì qī yǐ,
easily alarmed,
easily frightened,
easily pleased,
because their understanding is not thorough.
A guest asked Jìzǐ, saying:
"How did you know of Shùn's ability?"
Jìzǐ said:
"Yáo had already governed the world,
and Shùn's words on governing the world matched my own understanding,
therefore I knew of his ability."
"If you knew of his ability,
how did you know that he wouldn't act selfishly?"
Jìzǐ said:
"Those who can govern the world
must necessarily understand the true nature of life and destiny,
(those who understand the true nature of life and destiny,)
ought to be selfless.
In summer, one doesn't wear fur coats,
not because they don't like fur coats,
but because warmth is abundant.
In winter, one doesn't use a fan,
not because they don't like fans,
but because coolness is abundant.
A sage's not acting selfishly
is not because they love nobility,
but because they are disciplined within themselves.
"If one restrains oneself,
even the heart of greed will seem to stop,
how much more so a sage?"
Xǔ Yóu was not forced (jiāng)
but had something he understood.
With understanding, the lure of corruption is external.
The disciples and followers of Kǒng (Confucius) and Mò (Mozi) filled the world,
all teaching the arts of benevolence and righteousness throughout the land,
yet without success.
If the arts of the teachers themselves cannot be practiced,
how much less what they teach?
Why is this?
Because the arts of benevolence and righteousness are external.
To overcome the internal with the external,
a commoner cannot even walk on foot,
how much less a ruler?
Only by understanding the true nature of life
will the arts of benevolence and righteousness be practiced naturally.
The former kings could not know everything exhaustively,
they grasped the One and the myriad things were governed.
What makes people unable to grasp the One
is that they are moved by external things.
Therefore, it is said: "Remove the perversity of thought,
unravel the confusion of the heart,
eliminate the burdens on virtue,
clear the blockages of the Way."
Nobility, wealth, prominence, severity, reputation, and profit, these six
are things that go against one's intentions.
Appearance, movement, color, reason, energy, and intention, these six
are things that confuse one's heart.
Dislike, desire, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, these six
are things that burden virtue.
Wisdom, ability, departure, approach, taking, and relinquishing, these six
are things that obstruct the Way.
If these four sets of six are not churning about in one's breast, then one is correct.
Being correct leads to stillness,
stillness leads to clarity,
clarity leads to emptiness,
emptiness leads to non-action and yet nothing is left undone.
25.4 "Assigning Offices"
Four said:
The former kings employed those who did not possess it,
as if they themselves possessed it,
understanding the way of the ruler.
Now, the ruler,
dwells in emptiness (wears plain clothes) and possesses no wisdom,
therefore he is able to employ the wisdom of the many;
his wisdom is the opposite of ability,
therefore he is able to employ the abilities of the many;
his ability lies in upholding non-action,
therefore he is able to employ the actions of the many.
Without wisdom, without ability, without action,
This is what the lord holds onto.
What confuses the ruler is not like this.
To use his wisdom to strengthen wisdom,
to use his ability to strengthen ability,
to use his actions to strengthen actions,
this is the duty of a subordinate.
Occupying the position of a subordinate and desiring no obstruction,
even Shùn could not do it.
King Wǔ had five assistants.
King Wǔ was not capable in the affairs of these five assistants,
yet the world all said:
"The one who took the empire was King Wǔ."
Therefore, King Wǔ took what he did not possess,
as if it were his own,
he was in accord with the Way of the ruler.
Being in accord with the Way of the ruler,
then he can make the wise strategize,
he can make the brave become enraged,
he can make the eloquent speak.
Now, the horse,
Bólè assesses it,
Zàofù drives it,
the virtuous lord rides it,
it travels a thousand *lǐ* in a day.
Without the labor of driving and assessing, yet having its accomplishment,
then he knows what to ride.
Now, those who invite guests,
when the wine is flowing freely,
with singing, dancing, drumming, zithers, and playing the yu (竽),
the next day, they do not pay respect to those who brought them pleasure,
but pay respect to the host,
because the host directed them to do so.
The ancient kings establishing merit and fame
are similar to this.
They employ the capable and the virtuous,
and when great merit and fame are established in the world,
they do not give credit to those who assisted,
but give it to their lord,
because their lord directed them to do so.
It is like building a palace;
one must employ skilled craftsmen.
Why is that?
One says:
"If the craftsmen are not skilled, then the palace will not be well-built."
A state is a weighty matter.
If it is not well-governed,
how can it be compared to merely a poorly built palace?
When skilled craftsmen build a palace,
to make a circle, they must use a compass;
to make a square, they must use a set square;
to make something level and straight, they must use a level and plumb line.
Once the work is completed,
people do not recognize the compass, the set square, the level, and the plumb line,
but instead praise the skilled craftsmen.
Palaces are completed,
and (people) do not recognize the skilled artisans,
but all say:
"Good.
This is the palace of a certain lord or a certain king."
This is something that must be examined.
It is not so for a ruler who does not understand the way of rulership.
If he acts on his own, he will be unable (to govern).
If he employs the worthy, he will resent them.
If he consults with the unworthy,
this is how achievements are damaged,
and how the state is endangered.
Jujubes
belong to the thorn trees;
fur robes
belong to the foxes.
To eat jujubes from thorn trees,
to wear fox fur,
the former kings certainly used what they did not own,
and made it their own.
Tāng and Wǔ in one day completely possessed the people of Xià and Shāng,
completely possessed the land of Xià and Shāng,
completely possessed the wealth of Xià and Shāng,
because they made their people secure and no one in the world dared
to endanger them,
because they allocated their land and no one in the world dared not to be pleased,
because they rewarded with their wealth and everyone in the world eagerly encouraged (good behavior),
It was not through extravagance in Yī and Qí Zhōu
that the world praised them as greatly benevolent and greatly righteous;
the key lies in using what is not rightfully yours.
Bái Gōng Shèng obtained the state of Jīng,
but he was unwilling to distribute the wealth of its treasury among the people.
After seven days,
Shí Qǐ entered and said:
"Disaster is at hand!
If you are unwilling to distribute the wealth, then burn it,
lest people use it to harm us."
Bái Gōng still refused.
After nine days,
Yè Gōng entered,
and then he distributed the goods from the grand treasury among the masses,
and released the soldiers from the high storehouses to serve the people,
and thus attacked him.
After nineteen days, Bái Gōng died.
To want to possess a state that is not rightfully yours
can be called the height of greed;
to be unable to act for the benefit of others,
and also unable to act for your own benefit,
can be called the height of foolishness.
Bái Gōng's stinginess
is like an owl loving its own offspring.
Duke Líng of Wèi had a pond dug in the cold weather.
Wǎn Chūn remonstrated, saying:
"It is cold and the labor begins,
I fear it will harm the people."
The Duke said:
"Is it cold?"
Wǎn Chūn said:
"Your lord wears fox fur,
sits on a bear skin mat,
and in the corners are stoves,
therefore you are not cold.
Now the people wear tattered clothes that are not mended,
and worn-out shoes that are not repaired.
You, my lord, are not cold,
but the people are cold."
The Duke said:
"Good."
He ordered the labor to cease.
Those on the left and right remonstrated, saying:
"Your Lordship is digging a pond,
and does not know the coldness of the weather,
but Chūn knows it.
Because Chūn knows it, you order its cessation,
blessings will revert to Chūn,
and resentment will revert to the Duke."
The Duke said:
"Not so.
This Chūn,
is a commoner of the state of Lǔ,
and I have promoted him,
Now, the people have not seen it;
now, one will cause the people to see it in this way.
(He) said, "Moreover, Chūn has goodness superior to what I have;
is Chūn's goodness not my goodness?"
Líng Gōng's discussion of Wǎn Chūn,
can be said to understand the way of the ruler.
The ruler, indeed, has no personal responsibilities,
but receives responsibilities according to office.
Skill and clumsiness are the concerns of subordinates;
rewards and punishments are matters of law;
what business then does the ruler have?
If this is the case, then those who receive rewards have no merit,
and those who are executed have no grievance.
People reflect only on themselves;
this is the ultimate in good governance.
25.5 "Assignments"
Fifthly:
Whenever governing, one must first establish divisions.
Ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife;
when the six, ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, are in their proper positions,
then subordinates will not transgress rules, and superiors will not act carelessly,
the young will not be defiant and unruly, and the old will not be negligent and disrespectful.
Metal and wood have different tasks,
water and fire have distinct duties,
yin and yang are not the same,
yet they all benefit the people in the same way.
Therefore, it is through differences that one secures harmony;
it is through harmony that one endangers differences.
Distinctions between the same and the different,
distinctions between the noble and the lowly,
and the meaning of seniority and juniority,
these are what the former kings were cautious about,
and are the key to order and chaos.
Now, a shooter aims at a hair but misses the wall,
a painter models after a strand of hair but changes the face;
this speaks of the importance of examining the foundation.
If the foundation is not examined,
even Yáo and Shùn cannot govern with it.
Therefore, all chaos
must begin near and then reach far,
must begin with the root and then reach the branches.
Governance is also like this.
Therefore, Bǎi Lǐ Xī was in Yú and Yú perished,
was in Qín and Qín became dominant;
Xiàng Zhì was in Shāng and Shāng was destroyed,
was in Zhōu and Zhōu became kingly.
Bǎi Lǐ Xī's being in Yú,
was not because his wisdom was folly;
Xiàng Zhì's being in Shāng,
was not because his regulations were evil;
it was because they lacked the foundation.
His being in Qín,
was not because his wisdom was increased;
His position in the state of Zhou
was not due to him seeking favor;
it was because he had the fundamental qualities.
These fundamental qualities
are what is meant by having a clear sense of one's duties.
The state of Qi ordered Zhāng Zǐ to lead troops and attack Jing along with Han and Wei.
Jing ordered Táng Miè to lead troops and resist them.
The armies faced each other,
for six months without fighting.
Qi ordered Zhōu Zuì to urge Zhāng Zǐ to attack quickly,
his words were very harsh.
Zhāng Zǐ replied to Zhōu Zuì,
"To kill him, to dismiss him,
to destroy his family,
the king can obtain this from his subject.
To fight when it is not advantageous to fight,
to not fight when it is advantageous to fight,
the king cannot obtain this from his subject."
He encamped with the Jing people on opposite sides of the Ci River.
Zhāng Zǐ ordered men to scout for places where the river could be crossed,
the Jing people shot at them,
making it impossible to get near the water.
There was a man who gathered grass near the water,
who told the Qi scout,
saying:
"The water's depth is easy to discern.
The places the Jing people are guarding heavily,
They exhaust what is shallow;
what is selected for guarding,
are all the deep (places)."
A scout and a wood carrier met with Zhāng Zǐ,
Zhāng Zǐ was very pleased,
and then drilled his soldiers to launch a night raid on what the Jīng people heavily guarded,
and indeed killed Táng Miè.
Zhāng Zǐ can be said to have understood how to divide his forces.
Marquis Zhāo Xī of Hán went out hunting with arrows,
and the traces (of the chariot harness) were uneven and loose.
Marquis Zhāo Xī was in the chariot,
and said to his servant:
"Are the traces uneven and loose?"
His servant said:
"Yes."
Arriving at the lodge,
Marquis Zhāo Xī shot a bird,
and his attendant on the right adjusted one of the traces,
making it proper.
Marquis Zhāo Xī had already shot,
harnessed the chariot and returned,
got into the chariot,
and after a while,
said:
"Before, the traces were uneven and loose,
now they are proper,
why is that?"
His attendant on the right, following from behind, replied,
"Just now, your servant happened to go there."
The Marquis Zhāo Xī arrived,
and questioned the carriage driver.
Each avoided lodging (there).
Therefore, even if a self-asserted and reckless plan is correct,
a wise ruler will not follow it.
Now, if there is a person here,
who, by acting arbitrarily, can save the state,
and whose assessment of weights is like a balance,
and whose creation of squares and circles is like compass and square,
then this person is skilled and clever,
but not worth making a standard.
A standard is
what the multitude agree upon,
and it is how the worthy and unworthy exert their effort.
Plans that are unusable,
and affairs that cannot be agreed upon,
are what the former kings discarded.
25.6 《Careful About Small Things》
Six says:
Those above are honored and those below are humbled.
If one is humbled, then he is not allowed to view those above from a low perspective.
If one is honored, then he is indulgent,
and if he is indulgent, then he belittles small matters,
If light and small matters are not taken seriously, then those above will not understand those below.
Those below will not understand those above.
If those above and those below do not understand each other,
then those above will reject those below,
and those below will resent those above.
The feelings of ministers
cannot bear to be resented;
the feelings of rulers
cannot bear to love what they reject;
this is a great loss of the proper way between those above and those below.
Therefore, wise rulers are careful about small matters in order to discuss likes and dislikes.
A large dike that allows ants to burrow can flood towns and kill people;
ér piāo yì shā rén;
a sudden leak of a single spark
can burn down palaces and stored goods;
losing a single command
can result in the army being defeated and the commander dying;
a ruler making a single mistake in speech
can cause the country to be ruined and his reputation disgraced,
becoming a laughingstock for future generations.
Duke Xiàn of Wèi warned Sūn Lín Fù and Níng Zhí to eat.
Swans gathered in the park,
and the park keeper informed him.
The Duke went to the park to shoot swans.
The two men waited for the ruler,
the sun was late,
The duke did not come (to visit),
when he came, he did not remove his leather cap to meet the two sons.
The two sons were displeased,
so they drove out and presented (another) duke,
and established Gongzi Qián.
When Duke Zhuang of Wei was established,
he wanted to expel Shi Pu.
He ascended a platform to observe,
saw Rongzhou and asked about it, saying:
"What is this?"
An attendant said:
"It is Rongzhou."
Duke Zhuang said:
"I am of the Ji surname.
How dare Rong people reside in the state?"
He ordered that their houses be seized,
and their district ruined.
The Jin people happened to attack Wei,
so the people of Rongzhou, together with Shi Pu, killed Duke Zhuang,
and established Gongzi Qi.
This is a case of not paying attention to small matters.
People's inclinations do not stumble on mountains,
but stumble on anthills.
When Duke Huan of Qi ascended the throne,
he spoke three times in three years,
and the world called him virtuous,
and all the ministers were pleased.
Remove the flesh-eating beasts,
remove the grain-eating birds,
remove the silk nets and traps.
Wú Qǐ governed Xī Hé,
wishing to impress upon the people his trustworthiness.
One night, he placed a post outside the south gate
and proclaimed within the town,
"Tomorrow, whoever can knock down the post outside the south gate
will be appointed a senior official."
The next day, the sun was already late,
but no one had knocked down the post.
The people said to each other:
"This must not be true."
One person said:
"Let's try to knock down the post;
if we don't get a reward, so be it,
what harm is there?"
He went and knocked down the post
and came to see Wú Qǐ.
Wú Qǐ personally came out to meet him
and appointed him a senior official.
The next night, he again set up a post
and again proclaimed within the town as before.
The townspeople guarded the gate, vying for the post,
but the post was more firmly planted
and they did not receive the reward.
From that time on,
The people believed in Wú Qǐ’s rewards and punishments.
If rewards and punishments are believed by the people,
what cannot be accomplished?
Is it just in warfare?
Discussion on the Bearing of a Scholar, Sixth
26.1 *The Bearing of a Scholar*
It says:
A scholar is neither biased nor partisan,
gentle yet firm,
outwardly empty but inwardly substantial.
His appearance is clear but not flippant,
as if he has lost something important.
He disdains trivial matters but his ambition belongs to great things,
seemingly without courage but not easily frightened by fierce beasts,
his principles are firmly held and daring, and he cannot be insulted or harmed,
when facing calamity and hardship, he does not transgress righteousness,
even facing south and calling himself "the lonely one," he does not indulge in extravagance,
even ruling the people today and desiring to subdue foreign lands,
his frugality is very high and he does not rely on petty gains,
he disregards customs and can be relied upon to stabilize the world,
he does not seek wealth and rank, nor does he quickly depart from poverty and lowliness,
he values virtue and principle, and is ashamed to use clever defenses,
he is generous and tolerant beyond measure, but his core is very strict,
he is difficult to move with material things, and he will certainly not break his principles rashly.
This is the bearing of a scholar of the state.
In Qí, there was a man skilled at judging dogs.
His neighbor borrowed money (from the knowledgeable man) to buy a dog that would catch rats.
After a full year, he finally obtained one.
He said,
"This is a good dog."
His neighbor raised it for several years,
but it didn't catch any rats.
He told the dog judge about it.
The judge said,
"This is a good dog.
Its ambition lies in pursuing roe deer, elks, pigs, and deer,
not in rats.
If you want it to catch rats, then shackle it."
His neighbor shackled its hind legs,
and the dog then caught rats.
The spirit of a fine steed,
and the ambition of a swan,
are genuinely understood by the hearts of men.
People are also like this.
If sincerity exists within, then the spirit will respond to the person,
can words truly convey this?
This is called the unspoken word.
A guest came to see Tián Pián.
His clothing was in accordance with the proper rules,
his movements and retreats were within the proper measure,
his steps and flight were leisurely and refined,
and his speech was modest and quick.
Tián Pián listened to him completely and then declined him.
After the guest left,
Tián Pián saw him off with his eyes.
The disciples said to Tián Pián:
"Was that guest
a scholar?"
Tián Pián said:
"Probably not a scholar.
Now, what the guest emphasized on concealing,
is what a scholar strives to apply;
what a scholar emphasizes on concealing,
is what the guest strives to apply.
The guest is probably not a scholar."
Therefore, if a lamp illuminates one corner,
then the room is partially without light;
if bones and joints mature too early,
and the body's orifices cry out shrilly,
the body will certainly not grow tall;
if the masses have no plans for the future,
and only seek to be careful with what they see,
many disasters will result in misfortune;
if one's ambitions are not impartial,
one cannot achieve merit;
if one loves to gain but hates to give,
even if the state is large, one will not become king;
disasters will arrive daily.
Therefore, the appearance of a superior man
is as pure as jade from Mount Zhōng,
Like a stockade or prison, or a tree on a high hill.
Pure and diligent, cautious and fearful of change,
and unwilling to be content with themselves.
Diligent and pure, displeased with choices,
but with a heart that is very simple and honest.
Táng Shàng became a historian despite his age.
His old friends felt that Táng Shàng resented it,
thinking that Táng Shàng...
Táng Shàng said:
"It's not that I couldn't become a historian,
but I was ashamed and didn't want to."
His old friends did not believe him.
When Wei besieged Hándān,
Táng Shàng persuaded King Huì to lift the siege,
and gave the credit to Bó Yáng,
then his old friends believed that he was ashamed to be a historian.
After a time,
his old friends asked him to do something for his brother.
Táng Shàng said:
"When the ruler of Wei dies,
I will have your brother replace him."
His old friends rose and bowed again and believed him.
To disbelieve what is believable,
and to believe what is unbelievable,
this is the affliction of a fool.
To understand human nature,
but to be unable to forget oneself,
using this to rule,
Even if one possesses the world, what benefit is there?
Therefore, no defeat is greater than foolishness.
The trouble with foolishness
lies in the insistence on using only oneself.
If one uses only oneself, then boorish and ignorant people will follow and congratulate him.
To have a state like this
is worse than having none at all.
Antiquity and worthies
arise from this.
It's not that they hate their children and grandchildren,
nor that they seek and take pride in their name,
but rather it is to return to the reality [of the situation].
26.2 *Wù Dà*
Secondly:
Try to observe those of high ambition.
The assistants of the three kings,
their names were all without exception honored,
their realities were all without exception secure,
because their achievements were great.
The assistants of common lords,
their desires for name and reality are the same as those of the assistants of the three kings,
but their names are all without exception disgraced,
their realities are all without exception endangered,
because they have no merit.
They all worry that their own person is not valued in their state,
but they do not worry that their lord is not valued in the world;
This is why they desire honor, yet exceed in disgrace;
they desire safety, yet exceed in danger.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Swallows and sparrows contend for a good place under the same roof,
the mother and young feed each other,
they are content and happy in their small way,
thinking themselves safe.
The kitchen chimney collapses,
the upper beam burns,
the swallows' and sparrows' faces do not change color.
Why is this?
They do not know that disaster is about to befall them.
Are they not foolish!
Few ministers are more intelligent than these swallows and sparrows.
Those who are ministers,
advancing their rank, emoluments, wealth, and status,
fathers, sons, and brothers colluding together in one state,
content and happy in their small way,
thereby endangering their state,
are like the kitchen chimney being close to collapse,
and they never realize it to the end.
Their intelligence is no different from that of the swallows and sparrows.
Therefore, it is said:
'When the world is greatly disordered,
there is no safe state;
when one state is entirely disordered,
there is no safe family;
when one family is entirely disordered,
there is no safe self.'
This is what it means.
Therefore, the safety of the small
must depend on the large;
the safety of the large,
must depend on the small.
Small and large, lowly and noble,
mutually assist each other,
and then all can obtain what they enjoy."
Bó Yí persuaded Lord Sì of Wèi with the art of kingship.
Lord Sì responded, saying:
"What I possess is a thousand chariots;
I wish to receive your teachings."
Bó Yí answered, saying:
"Wū Huò can lift a thousand jun,
how much more easily one jīn?"
Dù Hè persuaded Lord Zhāo Wén of Zhōu with the goal of pacifying the empire.
Lord Zhāo Wén said to Dù Hè:
"I wish to learn how to pacify Zhōu."
Dù Hè answered, saying:
"If what I say is not right,
then I cannot pacify Zhōu;
if what I say is right,
then Zhōu will be pacified of itself."
This is what is meant by pacifying through non-pacification.
The ruler of Zhèng asked Bèi Zhān, saying:
"I have heard of your principle,
'Not dying for the ruler,'
'Not perishing for the ruler,'
is there truly such a thing?"
Bèi Zhān replied:
"There is.
If words are not heeded,
and the Way is not followed,
then certainly one does not serve the ruler.
If words are heeded and the Way is followed,
then why should one die or perish?"
Therefore, Bèi Zhān's not dying or perishing
is more virtuous than their dying or perishing.
In the past, Shùn desired to subdue those beyond the seas but did not succeed,
yet this was sufficient to become an emperor.
Yǔ desired to become an emperor but did not succeed,
yet this was sufficient to rule within the seas.
Tāng and Wǔ desired to succeed Yǔ but did not succeed,
yet this was sufficient to rule everywhere.
The Five Hegemons desired to succeed Tāng and Wǔ but did not succeed,
yet this was sufficient to be the leaders of the feudal lords.
Kǒng and Mò desired to implement the Great Way in the world but did not succeed,
If a grand principle is not achieved,
it already constitutes an achievement in itself,
therefore, strive for great things.
26.3 *Shàng Nóng*
It states:
The way in which the ancient sage kings guided their people
was to prioritize agriculture.
The reason for encouraging people to farm is not merely to exploit the land's resources,
yet this was sufficient to achieve prominence and honor.
but to value their spirit.
If the people farm, they will be simple;
if they are simple, they will be easy to employ;
if they are easy to employ, then the borders will be secure and
the ruler's position will be honored.
If the people farm, they will be stable;
if they are stable, they will have fewer selfish motives;
if they have fewer selfish motives, then public laws will be established and
their strength will be focused and unified.
If the people farm, their possessions will be abundant;
if their possessions are abundant, they will be reluctant to move;
if they are reluctant to move, they will die in their place without divided thoughts.
If the people abandon agriculture and pursue commerce, they will be unruly;
if they are unruly, they cannot be relied upon for defense;
they cannot be relied upon for battle.
If the people abandon agriculture and pursue commerce, their possessions will be diminished;
if their possessions are diminished, they will readily move;
if they readily move,
then when the state faces calamity,
all will have distant aspirations,
and none will have settled hearts.
If the people abandon agriculture and pursue commerce, they will be fond of cleverness;
When intelligence is favored, deception abounds;
when deception abounds, laws are skillfully manipulated,
making right into wrong,
and wrong into right.
Hòu Jì said:
"The reason for emphasizing farming and weaving
is to make them the fundamental teachings."
Therefore, the emperor personally leads the feudal lords in plowing the imperial fields,
and high officials and scholars all have achievements.
Therefore, in the affairs of that time,
agriculturalists were not given precedence in the state,
in order to teach the people to value land products.
The empress leads the nine consorts in silkworm rearing in the suburbs,
and mulberry planting on public land.
Therefore, in spring, autumn, winter, and summer, there were tasks involving hemp, flax, silk, and cocoons,
in order to encourage women to work.
Therefore, men do not weave but have clothes,
and women do not farm but have food,
men and women exchange their labor,
in order to prolong life;
this is the system of the sages.
Therefore, they revered time and cherished the days,
not resting until old age,
not ceasing unless ill,
and not stopping until death.
Superior fields,
A male laborer feeds nine people.
If the fields are poor,
a male laborer feeds five people.
One may increase (production),
but not decrease it.
One person manages it,
and ten people eat from it,
the six domestic animals are all included in this.
This is the way to heavily tax the land.
Therefore, the affairs of that time
did not include initiating earthworks,
or creating military expeditions,
commoners did not wear ceremonial caps, take wives, marry off daughters, or perform sacrifices,
did not gather crowds for drink and ritual.
The farmers’ needs were not reported to the authorities,
and they did not dare to privately register with laborers,
as it was detrimental to the times.
Then, establish the prohibitions of the countryside.
If they are not of the same clan,
farmers may not go out to serve in the military,
daughters may not marry outside (the clan),
in order to secure the farmers' livelihood.
There are five prohibitions of the countryside:
While the land has not yet been reclaimed,
do not process hemp,
do not carry out manure.
While my teeth have not grown long,
I dare not make gardens and parks.
Measuring my strength as insufficient,
I dare not dig canals to irrigate fields.
A farmer dares not engage in trade,
(I) dare not engage in unusual activities.
They are harmful to the seasons.
Then the prohibitions of the four seasons are established:
The mountains dare not be felled for timber, and trees are not cut down,
The people of the marshes dare not burn and plunder,
Snares and nets dare not go out the door,
Large nets dare not enter the deep waters,
The marshes, unless they are for boat patrols,
Dare not encroach for gain,
They are harmful to the proper time.
If the people do not exert themselves in farming,
And instead value domestic animals,
The state will be difficult to govern,
The three doubts will reach their peak,
This is called turning one's back on the root and reversing the norm,
Losing and destroying one's country.
All people from seven *chǐ* (feet) and above
Are assigned to the three offices.
Farmers focus on grain,
Artisans focus on tools,
Merchants focus on goods.
When timely actions are not shared,
this is called great misfortune.
If you deprive them of their work on the land,
this is called "delay,"
unending worry and complaining,
and you will surely lose their loyalty.
If you deprive them of their water management,
this is called "flute,"
loss following quickly after joy,
and the four neighboring areas will come empty.
If you deprive them of their military affairs,
this is called "danger,"
misfortune arising year after year,
and the sickle and artemisia will not be raised.
Repeatedly depriving the people of their time,
great famine will then come.
In the fields, there are resting plows,
some talking, some singing,
dawn then becomes dusk,
and lost grain is very much.
All know the branch,
none know its root and truth.
26.4 "Employing the Land"
Four say:
Hòu Jì said:
Can you make the hollow into a prominence?
Zǐ néng cáng qí è ér yī zhī yǐ yīn hū? Can you conceal their wickedness and greet them with deference?
Zǐ néng shǐ wú shì jìng ér qū yù shì hū? Can you make our soldiers tranquil and guide them to bathe the soldiers?
Zǐ néng shǐ bǎo shī ān dì ér chù hū? Can you make those who hold moisture at rest and the land safe to dwell in?
Zǐ néng shǐ guàn yí wú yín hū? Can you make the *guàn* barbarians not wander?
Zǐ néng shǐ zǐ zhī yě jǐn wèi líng fēng hū? Can you make the fields of your domain all become cool breezes?
Zǐ néng shǐ gǎo shù jié ér jīng jiān hū? Can you make the stalks have few nodes but strong stems?
Zǐ néng shǐ suì dà ér jiān, jūn hū? Can you make the ears of grain large, firm, and uniform?
Zǐ néng shǐ sù yuán ér báo kāng hū? Can you make the millet round with thin husks?
Zǐ néng shǐ mǐ duō wò ér shí zhī (jiāng) qiáng hū? Can you make the rice rich and, when eaten, strengthen [the eater]?
Wú zhī ruò hé? What is to be done without these things?
Fán gēng zhī dà fāng: In general, the grand method of cultivation:
Lì zhě yù róu, The strong desire gentleness,
róu zhě yù lì. The gentle desire strength.
Xī zhě yù láo, The rested desire labor,
láo zhě yù xī. The laborers desire rest.
Jí zhě yù féi, Barren land desires fertilizer,
féi zhě yù jí. Fertile land desires barrenness.
Jí zhě yù huǎn, Fast growing land desires slow growth,
huǎn zhě yù jí. Slow growing land desires fast growth.
Shī zhě yù zào, Damp land desires dryness,
zào zhě yù shī. Dry land desires dampness.
Shàng tián qì mǔ, The best fields should be given up (a portion) by the *mu* (area),
xià tián qì qū. The worst fields should be given up (a portion) by the *qu* (ditch).
Wǔ gēng wǔ nòu, Plow five times and weed five times,
bì shěn yǐ jìn. Be sure to scrutinize to the utmost.
Qí shēn zhí zhī dù, Regarding the degree to which it should be deeply planted,
yīn tǔ bì dé, Moist soil must be obtained,
Tall grasses do not grow,
and there are no rice-boring insects or water monsters.
This year, there is beautiful grain;
next year, there will be beautiful wheat.
Therefore, a six-foot plow
is used to cultivate a *mu*;
its width is eight inches,
which is used to make furrows;
the handle of the hoe is one foot,
this is its standard;
the hoe is six inches,
which is used to weed between crops.
The land can be made fertile,
and can also be made barren.
If you fertilize and plow, you must do it when it is damp,
so that the sprouts are strong and the soil has gaps;
if you hoe, you must do it when it is dry,
so that the land is fertile and the soil is loose.
The grass grows luxuriantly in the great month.
Fifty-seven days after the winter solstice,
the sweet flag begins to grow;
the sweet flag is the first of all plants to grow,
and then plowing begins.
In the past of early summer,
kill the three-leafed plants and harvest the wheat.
At the summer solstice,
the bitter vegetable dies and mushrooms grow,
And planting hemp and beans,
this tells the people that the earth's treasures are exhausted and dead.
All grass that grows hidden from the sun will come out,
the pig's head is born, and the wheat has no leaves,
and then one engages in storage,
this tells the people the limit.
At the five seasons, see the living and plant the living,
see the dead and harvest the dead.
The seasons of the world,
the land produces wealth,
but one does not consult with the people.
In a good year, bury earth (i.e., hoard grain),
in a bad year, bury earth (i.e., still hoard grain).
Do not miss the people's time,
do not let them govern it.
Those below know poverty, wealth, and useful tools,
all are made when the time comes,
and stopped when it is possible to stop.
Therefore, the strength of the old and weak can all be roused,
their use is (said to be) half a day,
their labor can be doubled.
Those who do not understand affairs,
resist it before the time has come,
admire it after the time has passed,
treat it lightly when it is the right time,
and make their people reject it.
Once the people reject it,
Nǎi yǐ liáng shí mù,
This is how things go when engaging in tasks below (standard).
If the work is harsh,
and one doesn't understand what's suitable for higher or lower ground,
then the people will move away.
Planting *lù* and *hé* (types of grain) and failing to treat them as *lù*,
planting heavy *hé* and failing to treat it as heavy (soil-appropriate),
results in little grain and wasted effort.
26.5 *Biàn Tǔ* (Distinguishing Soils)
Fifthly:
The principle of all cultivation is this:
It must begin with sandy soil,
because it dries out quickly due to its lack of moisture;
one must deeply bury the seeds in loamy soil,
because only by burying them deeply will they thrive;
loosen the cloddy soil,
plow the hard soil,
moisten the loamy soil before planting;
on upper (better) fields, spread out the fertilizer,
on lower (inferior) fields, use all the manure.
Do not let the three "thieves" control the land:
If the four seasons' cycles are not observed in the planting,
if the ditches are large and the furrows small,
making it like *qīng yú qū* (fish ribs, meaning sparse planting),
if the sprouts are like a straight hunt (meaning scattered),
then the land is stealing from you;
If one plants but does not tend
and cultivates but does not nourish growth,
then the seedlings will steal from each other.
If weeds are not removed, there will be wilderness;
if they are removed, there will be emptiness,
then the weeds will steal from the crops.
Therefore, if these three robbers are removed,
then grain can be abundant.
What is called present-day farming,
laboring without harvest, is this:
those that are planted too early are ahead of their time,
those that are planted too late miss the proper time,
cold and heat are not regulated,
the crops then suffer many disasters in their development.
They die in their substance.
Their misfortunes are that
if they are high and exposed, then moisture is lost;
if they are inclined, they are uneven;
if they are exposed to the wind, they are blown about;
if they are piled up high, they are pulled up;
in the cold, they wither;
in the heat, they become elongated.
At one time, five or six die.
Therefore, they cannot produce a future harvest.
They do not grow together, but they die together.
The failing crops die first,
and the many robbers then steal.
Wàng zhī sì yǒu yú,
but approaching it, it is emptiness.
The farmer knows that his field is easy to cultivate,
but does not know that his crops are sparse and unsuitable;
he knows that the boundaries of his field are weeded,
but does not know that the place where the crops reside is barren;
if not weeded, it becomes overgrown,
if weeded, it becomes barren,
this is the harm of the matter.
Therefore, the field should be wide and level,
the channels should be small, deep, and clear;
the bottom receives shade (yin),
the top receives sunlight (yang),
and then everything grows.
Crops should grow from dust,
and be planted in firmness.
Be careful with the seeds,
do not make them too numerous,
nor make them too sparse.
Regarding applying soil,
do not make it insufficient,
nor make it excessive.
When thoroughly harrowing,
be sure to focus on mounding the soil around the plants.
Harrowing makes them upright,
and those that are upright will surely sprout first.
Applying soil evenly,
For grains to grow evenly, they must certainly be planted densely.
Therefore, the fields should be broad and level,
so that the root stalks are not damaged.
When planting in the earth,
divide into five sections by the earth.
Stalks should grow in rows,
so that they grow quickly;
the weak should not harm each other,
so that they grow large quickly.
Horizontal rows must be measured,
vertical rows must be planned.
Straighten the rows,
allow the wind to pass through,
open up the center of the heart (of the field),
and create a cooling breeze.
Seedlings, when they are weak, want to be isolated,
when they are growing, they want to live together,
when they are ripe, they want to support each other.
Therefore, plant in groups of three,
then there will be much grain.
Generally, the trouble with grain is
not that they all grow and die together.
Therefore, those that grow first produce good rice,
those that grow later become chaff.
Therefore, when weeding,
nourish the elder stalks and remove the younger ones.
When the soil is fertile, do not let supporting stalks become sparse,
Barren trees do not want to grow alone but live in groups.
If fertilized and not thinned, there will be much chaff;
if barren and living alone, there will be much death.
Those who do not understand farming:
when weeding, they remove the older plants and nourish the younger,
they do not harvest the millet but harvest the chaff,
those above and below are not at peace,
then the grain will die.
In thick soil, shoots cannot spread,
in thin soil, plants grow rampant but do not flourish.
Dark color of coarse clay,
hard soil, soft seeds,
avoid tilling, kill the hidden,
so that farming succeeds.
26.6 "Judging the Seasons"
Six says:
The way of farming,
thickness is treasured:
cutting trees at the wrong time,
if not broken, the grain will surely be damaged;
if the crops are ready but not harvested,
one will surely encounter natural disasters.
Farming, what makes it happen is people,
what gives it life is the earth,
what nourishes it is heaven.
Therefore, people's farming allows for feet,
Hoeing looks like hoeing,
grasping looks like grasping.
This is called the Way of farming.
Therefore, rice that is planted at the right time
grows tall and has full ears,
with large roots and stems that are killed off,
with sparse stalks and large ears;
its grains are round and have thin husks;
its rice is very fertile and eating it makes one (strong) vigorous;
such rice does not get blown away (by the wind).
Rice planted before the right time
has stems and leaves that are awned and short in length,
with large ears but diminished fragrance,
separated rice but no aroma.
Rice planted after the right time
has stems and leaves that are awned but short,
with full ears but green and sparse,
much chaff but not full.
Millet that is planted at the right time
has awned stems that droop downwards,
with awned ears that are long,
with round grains and thin husks,
easy to hull,
and eating it is not cloying and is fragrant;
such millet is not glutinous.
Millet planted before the right time
A large root with luxuriant foliage,
if the stalk is injured, it will not thrive.
The leaves will be withered, and the ear short.
If it matures late,
the stalk will be small, and the hemp long,
the ear short, and the chaff thick,
the millet will be tightly packed and without fragrance.
Rice that matures in season
will have a large root with a flourishing stalk,
long *tóng* with sparse grains,
the ear like a horse's tail,
the grain large and without awns,
the rice plump with thin chaff,
easy to husk and fragrant to eat;
rice like this will not cause indigestion.
If it matures early,
the root will be large, but the stalks and leaves will be stiffly aligned,
the *tóng* short, and the ear short,
much chaff, and thick husks,
little rice and many awns.
If it matures late,
the stalks will be thin and will not grow,
the chaff thick, with much blighted grain, and the rice uneven,
unable to rely on its full maturity,
it will die looking up to the heavens.
Hemp that matures in season
If wheat awns are long,
with sparse nodes and a yellowish color,
a small base and sturdy stalks,
thick chaff evenly distributed,
ripening late with abundant grain,
and growing both day and night;
such wheat will not suffer from locusts.
Soybeans that ripen at the proper time
have long stems and short roots;
their beautiful pods grow in clusters of fourteen,
with many branches and numerous nodes,
competing in foliage and abundant fruit;
large soybeans are round,
small soybeans are round and fragrant;
when weighed, they are heavy,
when eaten, they are satisfying and fragrant;
such soybeans will not suffer from insects.
Those that ripen too early
must grow long with vines,
floating leaves and sparse nodes,
with small flowers and barren pods.
Those that ripen too late
have short stems and sparse nodes,
and an empty, barren base.
Wheat that ripens at the proper time
has long awns and a black neck,
growing in rows of fourteen,
and is suitable,
with thin husks and a reddish color,
when weighed, it is heavy,
when eaten, it is very fragrant and satisfying,
making one's skin smooth and strong;
